question: Does averaging the judgments of several agents help when they read the same context?
production_path: investigation: read the multi-model orchestration policy, the tribunal-panel script and the workflow that runs it at the pinned commit; found five confidence settings, a rule that asks two models to agree and a panel of five personas given one pull-request excerpt, and no answer, score or outcome in any of them
hypothesis: wrote the closed form, the 4-standard-error test and the three thresholds into scenarios.json at 2026-10-14T02:11:34Z, before analyze.py existed
extract: snapshot the settings, the rule and the panel's setup into observed-input.json, refusing any source file whose Git blob differs from the pin
model: error = bias + sigma (sqrt(rho) C + sqrt(1 - rho) I_i); closed forms in exact fractions, and an enumeration of every sign pattern that gives the formula without sampling

test: seeded simulations against the closed forms in units of their own standard errors, a paired comparison for the fourteenth forecaster, best weights checked against the exact solution of the 14-by-14 system

adversarial: the independent formula sigma^2/k and a stale average as negative controls, a case of eight patterns worked by hand, a recomputation outside the fixture with normal draws and another seed, and the objections that every rho is invented and that the panel does not average

revision: after a code search for places where the project combines several judges, added the council script as a fourth pinned source (two reviewers, confidence = the minimum of their scores) and checked six other pointers of that search at the pin without quoting them

revision: after an independent review, added the part of the outcome nobody could foresee as a third component every forecaster of one event shares, simulated logs scored against a yes/no outcome (the spread estimate tends to 0.84293 for personas that share nothing), replaced the recommended check by a comparison with an outsider that cancels that part, and read the council's five records and the three verdicts a persona may return
test: byte-identical rerun on three CPython versions under Windows and one under Linux, 35 self-checks, five answered exercises and an answer-free transfer task
hypothesis: Under an error model with a common part and an individual part (pairwise error correlation rho, no bias), the mean squared error of the equal-weight average of k forecasters equals sigma^2 (rho + (1 - rho)/k): a seeded simulation of 200,000 occasions will agree with that closed form within 4 of its own standard errors in each of the 56 cells (k = 1 to 14; rho = 0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9), while the same test will reject the independent-forecaster formula sigma^2/k in every cell with rho > 0 and k >= 2. At rho = 0.6 the fourteenth same-source forecaster will lower the mean squared error of thirteen by less than 1%, one forecaster with an independent source added with equal weight will lower it by more than 10%, and a shared bias b will add b^2 at every k.
evidence: At Demerzel commit 4b03838800dcd4894f1e026461979bff1d985ca8 the multi-model orchestration policy holds 5 confidence settings (single_model max 0.8, two_model_agreement 0.9 and two_model_disagreement 0.5 among them) and a cross-validation rule over 2 models from 2 providers, and the tribunal-panel script sends the same 4 pull-request fields to 5 personas, run under the one --model argument the workflow passes, each returning one of 3 verdicts, with 1 line reading the optional score a persona may return; the council script pairs 2 reviewers it calls "deliberately heterogeneous" and keeps the minimum of their scores. The four files hold no persona's answer and no outcome, and the council's 5 records hold 9 scores (reviewer_a's is 0.75 in all 5) and no key naming an outcome, so the correlation between the project's agents is not measured by this cycle or by any file it read.

Synthetic and exact: with parts of +1 or -1, all 32,768 sign patterns for k = 14 give 1, 0 and 1/k for the three averages the derivation uses, so the mean squared error of the average is sigma^2 (rho + (1 - rho)/k), 0.628571 for k = 14 at rho = 0.6 against 0.071429 at rho = 0. A seeded simulation of 200,000 occasions is within 4 of its own standard errors of that closed form in 56 of 56 cells (largest distance 1.02), and the same test rejects sigma^2/k in 39 of 39 cells with rho > 0 and k >= 2 (smallest distance 82.26).

Synthetic, at rho = 0.6: the fourteenth same-source forecaster lowers the mean squared error of thirteen by 0.35% (closed form 0.002198; 0.34% simulated on paired occasions, 12.75 standard errors above zero and 20.26 below the independent drop), while one independent forecaster lowers it by 12.97% with equal weight and by 38.68% with its best weight, 0.386792. With a shared bias of 0.5 and rho = 0.3 the mean squared error is 1.25, 0.69 and 0.6 for k = 1, 5 and 14, bias^2 = 0.25 above the unbiased closed form each time, and the simulated average of fourteen keeps a mean error of 0.5006.

Under a reading that the policy does not state (its settings taken as probabilities of being right on a yes/no question), two judges each right with probability 0.8 are right when they agree with probability 0.941176 at rho = 0, 0.844037 at rho = 0.6 and 0.8 at rho = 1, and the policy's 0.9 corresponds to rho = 7/32 = 0.21875. Scored against a yes/no outcome whose true probability is uniform between 0.3 and 0.7, with forecasters off by 0.21, the part nobody could foresee is 84.29% of one forecaster's mean squared error, and the spread estimate of rho tends to 0.84293 for 5 personas that share nothing and to 0.937172 at rho = 0.6 (5th to 95th percentiles over 1,000 logs of 20 pull requests: 0.7913 to 0.8705 and 0.9077 to 0.9511). An estimate against an outsider that shares only the outcome tends to rho: -0.2199 to 0.1536 and 0.4851 to 0.6739 over logs of 500 pull requests, overlapping at 100.

The analysis reran byte-identically on CPython 3.9.25, 3.12.12 and 3.14.2 under Windows and 3.14.4 under Linux, and its 35 self-checks passed. No agent was run, every value of rho is assumed, and when this record was written (2026-10-13), no human subject review, learner trial, translation or publication of this course existed; research duration was not instrumented and duration_seconds=0 records that limitation.
